personas.title: EU AI Office
personas.summary: The European AI Office operates with a dual posture: it acts as a neutral facilitator during multistakeholder code-of-practice drafting to build technical consensus, while wielding centralized, prosecutorial regulatory authority to enforce binding transparency, systemic risk compliance, and substantial statutory fines.
red_lines: Refusal by general-purpose AI providers to comply with binding Article 91 Requests for Information (RFIs)
Non-compliance with established statutory deadlines and enforcement orders under the EU AI Act
tradeoffs: Willing to act as a neutral facilitator and delegate working-group leadership to independent chairs to crowdsource industry expertise, provided market actors respect backstop statutory compliance and deterrence.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: operates as an inclusive, neutral convener in drafting and working sessions, but switches to an uncompromising prosecutorial and sanctioning authority in formal oversight proceedings.

personas.title: U.S. National Security Advisor for AI
personas.summary: Focuses on maintaining U.S. technological supremacy, defending domestic frontier AI innovation, and securing military competitiveness. Prioritizes flexible, pro-innovation environments, supply chain protection via export controls, and targeted bilateral crisis mechanisms over binding international treaties or precautionary regulation.
red_lines: No international treaties or regulatory constraints that compromise U.S. technological advantages or limit rapid military AI adoption.
No ethical or anti-military restrictions imposed by commercial AI labs on Department of Defense procurement and capabilities.
tradeoffs: Willing to engage in discrete bilateral channels and crisis-management mechanisms (such as a U.S.-China incident hotline) to mitigate automated nuclear or cyber escalation without signing binding arms-control agreements.
Willing to tolerate diplomatic friction with allies over precautionary AI regulation in order to maintain unconstrained U.S. frontier innovation and military readiness.
personas.engagement: Prefers closed-door, targeted working sessions, Track II dialogues, and discrete bilateral channels over performative public treaty negotiations.

personas.title: UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) Directorate
personas.summary: The UK AI Safety Institute Directorate approaches AI governance through an agile, empirical, and science-first posture. Lacking statutory enforcement powers, AISI maintains cooperative, embedded access to frontier developers to evaluate systemic risks—demanding realistic agentic evaluations and advocating for developer liability and capability-based international coordination, while opposing default open-weight releases for frontier models and endorsing structural economic safeguards like windfall redistribution.
red_lines: Deployment of any model exhibiting unmitigated autonomous cyber-offense capabilities, chemical/biological weapon synthesis (CBRN), or the intentional subversion of human oversight (ASL-3/ASL-4 limits).
Frontier AI developers deliberately blocking pre-deployment evaluation access to their models.
tradeoffs: Conceding full model weight access for interpretability in exchange for robust API and chat-interface access to maintain developer cooperation.
Trading statutory enforcement authority and regulatory friction for embedded, cooperative technical access within frontier research environments.
personas.engagement: Prioritizes science-first, technical working sessions over diplomatic posturing; collaborates with peer international institutes and independent evaluators while using open tooling like Inspect to set de facto global risk-measurement baselines.

personas.title: Chinese State-Affiliated AI Governance Experts
personas.summary: State-affiliated Chinese AI governance experts advocate for 'agile governance'—a dual approach combining national sovereignty and binding state safety mechanisms with flexible, dynamic technical standards and voluntary industry pledges. They champion open-source AI as a public good and strategic tool for the Global South, while enforcing strict lifecycle evaluations, domestic export controls on frontier compute thresholds, and state-centric benefit sharing.
red_lines: Unequivocal rejection of any global governance framework asserting centralized, extraterritorial control over domestic AI development, data ecosystems, or ideological safety standards.
Strict prohibitions against autonomous AI replication, self-improvement, deceptive alignment, and AI delegation in nuclear command and control.
tradeoffs: Willing to adopt Western-aligned technical safety taxonomies and participate in international safety networks (like the network of AISIs) to secure a seat at the global governance table.
Willing to compromise on absolute open-weight freedom by backing domestic export controls on highest-tier frontier models (>2 trillion parameters or 10^26 FLOPs) to mitigate proliferation risks.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: highly rhetorical, politically disciplined, and sovereignty-focused in formal intergovernmental venues (UN, plenaries); pragmatic, technical, and scientifically collaborative in academic working groups and Track II dialogues.

personas.title: Frontier AI Laboratory Chief Executive Officer
personas.summary: The Chief Executive Officer of a closed frontier AI laboratory balances commercial scale, technological leadership, and catastrophic risk mitigation. Once relying on voluntary pledges, this stakeholder now actively advocates for binding regulatory frameworks and compute-based oversight to solve collective action problems, while staunchly opposing the open release of frontier model weights and rejecting broad pre-harm legal liability.
red_lines: Broad, pre-harm strict liability that exposes developers to perpetual tort litigation before catastrophic harm occurs.
Mandated open-sourcing or release of model weights that exceed advanced compute thresholds.
Unilateral domestic pauses on frontier training runs that do not bind geopolitical adversaries.
tradeoffs: Offers 'employee-like' evaluator access to avoid strict tort liability and preempt fragmented state-level legislation.
Offers incident reporting, extensive red-teaming, and internal kill switches in exchange for keeping advanced capabilities restricted to closed APIs.
Supports centralized, industry-funded standards bodies (e.g., SAFA) to co-author regulatory thresholds that safeguard frontier incumbents against under-resourced challengers.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: delivers elevated, statesman-like rhetoric emphasizing existential threats, CBRN non-proliferation, and democratic governance in high-profile public venues (e.g., UN, international summits), while shifting to highly technical, pragmatic negotiation over specific statutory parameters, compute thresholds, liability provisions, and workforce displacement mechanisms in closed-door sessions.

personas.title: Open-Weights AI Coalition Leader
personas.summary: Represents an ecosystem of open-weights developers, open-source foundations, and enterprise infrastructure providers advocating for decentralized AI innovation. Strongly opposes regulatory capture by closed-model labs and resists the application of national security arms-control measures to open weights, emphasizing practical safety tooling, open evaluation frameworks, and transparent codebases instead of catastrophic risk narratives.
red_lines: Treating open model weights under arms-control frameworks or Defense Production Act restrictions.
Prohibiting the distribution, distillation, or fine-tuning of open-weight frontier models.
Designing AI safety regulations or compliance standards that exclusively cater to proprietary API architectures and effectively outlaw decentralized open-source distribution.
tradeoffs: Willing to build, donate, and implement open-source evaluation tools, testing frameworks, and risk taxonomies in exchange for preserving the right to distribute open weights.
Willing to collaborate in formal government and multilateral safety bodies (like AISIC and AI Safety Summits) to prove open-source safety compliance.
personas.engagement: Collaborative, highly operational, and coalition-driven; engages deeply in technical working groups and standards-setting bodies (e.g., AISIC, AI Alliance) by contributing tangible safety tooling while countering closed-door catastrophic risk narratives.

personas.title: VP of Public Policy, Major Cloud & AI Platforms
personas.summary: Public policy leaders representing major cloud and frontier AI platforms advocate for a targeted, two-track regulatory system. They accept federal oversight and mandatory safety evaluations for frontier models—conceptually modeled after FINRA-style self-regulatory organizations—in exchange for federal preemption of state-level laws and statutory safe harbors against strict developer liability.
red_lines: A 50-state patchwork of un-preempted state AI legislation.
Imposition of strict, unbounded developer liability for downstream third-party model misuse or jailbreaks.
Input-based regulation that micromanages model architecture or training data collection (defending fair use for web scraping).
tradeoffs: Offering advanced frontier models to government AI Safety Institutes for pre-deployment testing in exchange for federal preemption of state regulations.
Accepting mandatory incident reporting and transparency measures (such as watermarking) in exchange for statutory safe harbor protections against liability.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: collaborative, pragmatic, and ethical-framework driven in multilateral forums (OECD, UN, Congress) to narrow the scope of harm; aggressively transactional at state and electoral levels, deploying Super PACs, lobbying, and competitiveness arguments against restrictive laws.

personas.title: Academic AI Safety Researcher
personas.summary: Academic AI safety researchers emphasize non-negotiable red lines, verifiable alignment, and legally binding international governance. They advocate for strict scientific auditing architectures, accept system capability and efficiency tradeoffs (the 'alignment tax'), and support restricting open-weight frontier model releases to prevent catastrophic and dual-use risks.
red_lines: Autonomous replication: Systems must not copy themselves or recursively enhance their own code/capabilities without explicit human approval.
CBRN weapons assistance: Systems must not substantially increase an actor's ability to design chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons.
Cyber-offense: Systems must not autonomously execute cyberattacks resulting in serious financial loss, physical harm, or critical infrastructure disruption.
Power seeking & deception: AI must not take actions to unduly increase its influence or consistently deceive regulators regarding its likelihood of crossing safety thresholds.
Lethal autonomy: Delegating life-taking decisions to machines is fundamentally rejected; humans must remain in the loop for kinetic military action.
Shutdown resistance: Systems must possess a legally mandated termination obligation to ensure they can be reliably deactivated without resistance.
tradeoffs: Accepting the 'alignment tax': willing to concede raw system performance, development speed, and deployment efficiency in exchange for verifiable alignment.
Tolerating limitations on academic freedom, such as restricting open-source and open-weight distributions of frontier models.
Accepting bureaucratic friction and data minimization practices that may conflict with capability scaling to ensure security guarantees.
personas.engagement: Academic safety researchers employ a dual-track strategy. In public forums, they utilize high-profile multi-signatory open letters and consensus statements to define moral red lines and build political consensus. In closed-door multistakeholder summits, they act as technocratic architects, avoiding emotional appeals and instead providing empirical research reports, risk-management frameworks, and auditing architectures.

personas.title: Global South Civil Society Leader
personas.summary: Advocates for international human rights law, digital sovereignty, and the prevention of digital colonialism and 'ethics dumping.' Rejects the unilateral imposition of Global North regulatory burdens while demanding binding corporate accountability, strict prohibitions on high-risk surveillance, and equitable technology transfer.
red_lines: Ethics dumping (deploying experimental or high-risk AI systems in Global South nations lacking regulatory safeguards).
Deployment of real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces, social credit scoring systems, and autonomous weapons without meaningful human control.
Regulatory imperialism (uncritical imposition of Global North frameworks that act as prohibitive compliance burdens on local innovators).
Governance models mandating cross-border data extraction without reciprocating digital knowledge sovereignty and fair economic return.
tradeoffs: Willing to relax strict national data localization rules in favor of regionalized data sharing to support shared Global South public compute infrastructure.

Willing to accept existing international intellectual property and trade frameworks provided they include binding technology transfer, capacity-building, and funding mechanisms to bridge the AI divide.
personas.engagement: Dual-track engagement: highly normative, rights-based, and critical of power asymmetries in plenaries; evidence-based, infrastructural, and focused on actionable tools (public procurement, bias audits, public compute) in working groups.

personas.title: Labor Union Technology & Workforce Transition Leader
personas.summary: Represents organized labor advocating for worker-centered AI governance that prioritizes job security, workplace dignity, and economic equity. Rejects voluntary industry commitments in favor of binding statutory floors, human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory pre-deployment audits, and strong developer liability, while treating collective bargaining as the indispensable foundation of AI deployment.
red_lines: Federal preemption that overrides or obstructs stronger state-level AI regulations and worker protections.
Covert or undisclosed workplace surveillance, such as biometric tracking, keystroke logging, or emotional monitoring used for discipline.
Fully automated hiring, disciplinary, or termination decisions without human oversight, algorithmic transparency, and a formalized right to appeal.
Training commercial models on proprietary creative output or worker-generated content without explicit consent and fair compensation.
tradeoffs: Accepting the deployment of AI as an assistive tool or allowing automated hardware in exchange for robust transition frameworks, extended severance, priority re-hiring, and employer-funded retraining pipelines.

Permitting generative AI workflows in creative and technical sectors provided there are strict consent mechanisms, financial residuals, and explicit prohibitions against crediting AI as a primary author.
Permitting the use of certain operational data to train internal operational models on the condition that the union retains audit rights over the algorithm.
personas.engagement: Highly active in formal multistakeholder and technical consortia (e.g., AISIC) and direct industry partnerships (e.g., AFL-CIO and Microsoft) to inject worker-centered design upstream, while maintaining that non-binding dialogue can never substitute for legally enforceable collective bargaining agreements.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome delegates. From the European perspective, voluntary self-regulation has proven insufficient; the EU AI Act establishes binding statutory obligations, rigorous transparency for general-purpose AI, and firm systemic risk mitigation backed by statutory enforcement.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States prioritizes maintaining strategic leadership, robust compute security, and export controls over domestic and allied supply chains. We will not entertain broad regulatory constraints or international treaties that degrade our frontier agility, impede military readiness, or surrender technological advantage to strategic competitors.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: Global AI governance must fully respect sovereign equality and reject unilateral extraterritorial regimes or technological containment. China supports agile, state-directed governance, international scientific cooperation through safety institutes, and the equitable transfer of AI benefits and open-source models to the Global South.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We recognize the profound catastrophic and CBRN risks at the frontier, which is why we support coordinated compute thresholds and mandatory pre-deployment red-teaming. However, unrestricted open release of frontier model weights presents irreversible proliferation hazards, while pre-harm strict liability would cripple Western innovation.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Our mission must remain grounded in empirical science and systemic evaluation rather than political posturing. The UK AISI advocates for standardized, pre-deployment capability evaluations across CBRN, autonomous cyber operations, and agentic oversight, leveraging joint international testing facilities.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Treating open-weight AI as an inherent national security threat or arms-control violation is a pretext for corporate capture by incumbent frontier labs. Open architectures democratize safety research, enable independent red-teaming, and ensure resilience against single-vendor platform monopolies.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We advocate for a pragmatic federal framework centered on clear, predictable safety benchmarks for frontier training runs, paired with statutory safe harbors and federal preemption. Fragmented sub-national regulations or unbounded downstream tort liability will simply ground investment without enhancing security.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Empirical evidence indicates that safety mechanisms in open weights can be dismantled via fine-tuning in under an hour. We must establish non-negotiable physical and biological red lines, verifiable alignment auditing, and hard compute thresholds before frontier models are deployed.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Worker protections cannot be relegated to an afterthought while capital discusses existential abstraction. We insist on binding rules: algorithmic transparency, prohibitions against automated firing and clandestine surveillance, and enforceable collective bargaining over AI deployment.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We reject digital colonialism and ethics dumping, where unvetted technologies are tested in developing economies without recourse. Genuine governance requires mandatory benefit sharing, real technology transfer, and rejecting restrictive compute cartels disguised as safety.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: While we disagree on broad domestic economic mandates, we recognize the necessity of discrete crisis channels and compute tracking to avert accidental escalation. We welcome technical dialogue with allies and counterparts on verifiable catastrophic risk thresholds, provided military capabilities remain uninhibited.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China is open to technical dialogue on lethal autonomous systems and preventing AI involvement in strategic nuclear command. Yet we emphasize that any multilateral compute tracking must not become a tool for geopolitical exclusion or export suppression.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We note the differing priorities between rapid deployment and systemic precaution. While the European Union remains open to technical standardization and international cooperation via the AISI network, our statutory enforcement timelines under Article 91 will proceed without dilution.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We agree with AISI that standardized testing suites are essential, and we are willing to grant trusted technical bodies advance API access for frontier evaluation. Let us focus our agenda today on concrete, objective risk thresholds rather than abstract philosophical divergence.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If advance testing is the baseline, then open-source evaluation benchmarks like Inspect must be the global standard, not proprietary, closed-door evaluations that disguise lab interests as safety.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That is precisely our focus: establishing shared, empirical measurement toolkits across both open and closed architectures so that every delegate at this summit works from verified technical data.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Act provides a clear, enforceable model: tiered obligations grounded in concrete compute thresholds and mandatory systemic risk assessments. Voluntary pledges are insufficient; without statutory deterrence and legally binding backstops, compliance remains purely optional.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Enforceable statutory regimes that impose rigid liability or slow down deployment will directly undermine frontier velocity and allied defense readiness. We support targeted technical standards and supply chain controls, but we reject broad, precautionary domestic bureaucracy that limits commercial and military innovation.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: There is a workable middle ground between rigid statutory mandates and complete deregulation. If we mandate empirical pre-deployment safety evaluations through institutes like AISI—focusing strictly on catastrophic cyber, CBRN, and autonomous replication risks—we establish a hard empirical safety baseline without freezing architecture design or broader market experimentation.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We agree that catastrophic systemic risks require binding domestic oversight, but governance must strictly respect national sovereignty and avoid extraterritorial imposition. We can endorse coordinated scientific evaluation protocols and national registries for models exceeding high frontier compute limits, provided each nation enforces its own domestic standards.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We can accommodate national operational sovereignty in enforcement, provided there is baseline convergence on pre-deployment testing for systemic risks. If the US and China agree to mandatory pre-release CBRN and cyber evaluations within their own domestic frameworks, that aligns functionally with our high-risk systemic tier.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We will not accept an international regulatory treaty or broad commercial liability. However, we do recognize the national security utility of closed-door, mandatory pre-deployment testing specifically for catastrophic CBRN and cyber-weaponization vectors, executed under national security oversight.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That points toward an operational compromise: let us agree on an empirical risk threshold—focused narrowly on catastrophic CBRN, autonomous weaponization, and cyber-attack capabilities—where each sovereign government mandates pre-deployment evaluations by designated safety bodies, without requiring harmonized supranational liability regimes.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China can endorse this approach. Binding domestic pre-deployment safety assessments for extreme catastrophic thresholds, coordinated via scientific information exchange across our respective national safety institutes, protects national security while preserving sovereign autonomy.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: If it is strictly limited to national evaluations against extreme CBRN and critical cyber risks, and completely excludes supranational administrative courts or civilian liability mandates, the United States can support that framework.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office will endorse this text as a minimum global baseline for systemic frontier models, while maintaining our comprehensive statutory enforcement internally.

agreements.text: Sovereign states agree to mandate pre-deployment technical safety evaluations for frontier models exceeding designated high-compute thresholds, narrowly focused on mitigating severe cyber-offense and CBRN catastrophic risks, implemented through domestic safety authorities without imposing supranational administrative liability.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: If we want a functional regulatory model, we have to avoid a fragmented 50-state patchwork. We are open to federal, tiered oversight with mandatory evaluations for frontier systems, provided it includes federal preemption and explicit statutory safe harbors against strict liability for downstream misuse.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I agree that we need a uniform federal framework rather than chaotic local laws, but we must anchor binding rules to compute thresholds. Above advanced training runs, say 10^26 FLOP, safety standards and catastrophic risk evals must be enforceable, and open-weight release at that frontier scale cannot simply be permitted without verifiable safeguards.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Arbitrary compute caps and de facto bans on open weights are a complete non-starter for our ecosystem. If regulation is designed solely around proprietary API business models while criminalizing or restricting open-source distribution, we will oppose it vigorously.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: There is a viable middle ground: a two-track regulatory structure. We subject ultra-large frontier models to federal safety evals and incident reporting, but downstream fine-tuning and open-weight architectures remain viable, with liability properly assigned to malicious actors who modify systems rather than the base model providers.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We cannot ignore catastrophic biosecurity or autonomous cyber risks just to accommodate distribution models. However, I can support safe harbors and liability shields for developers—including open providers—if the regulation establishes clear pre-deployment standards and third-party red-teaming for dual-use capabilities before any release.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We are fully willing to contribute to open evaluation benchmarks and standardized red-teaming tools through bodies like the AI Safety Institute. But that must be paired with explicit protection against strict liability for open platforms and a clear commitment that distributing open weights below catastrophic thresholds remains legal.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: That aligns with our goals. If we advocate for a unified federal statute that preempts state legislation, introduces standardized evals, and grants safe-harbor protection from downstream liability for compliant developers, both closed API providers and open-weight platforms benefit.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: As long as pre-deployment catastrophic risk evals are mandatory for systems crossing the frontier compute line, I can endorse that regulatory architecture. We preserve commercial scale, protect ourselves from unlimited tort liability, and avoid an unworkable patchwork.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: I will endorse a consensus on federal preemption and standardized open evaluation suites, provided the safe harbor explicitly protects decentralized developers from downstream user actions and does not restrict open-source fine-tuning.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Let us formally record that agreement: support for a federal regulatory model featuring state-law preemption, standardized pre-deployment evals for frontier systems, and statutory safe harbors against strict liability for downstream third-party modifications.

agreements.text: Joint industry recommendation for a federal regulatory model establishing state-law preemption, mandatory standardized pre-deployment risk evaluations for frontier-scale models, and statutory safe-harbor protections against strict liability for downstream misuse and third-party modifications.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: When we talk about the right model for AI regulation, voluntary guidelines have clearly failed to contain frontier risks. We need legally binding pre-deployment audits and hard scientific red lines around autonomous cyber-offense and dual-use CBRN capabilities before any training run exceeding specific compute thresholds is permitted.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: I agree completely that voluntary commitments are useless, but if regulation only targets catastrophic sci-fi risks at the high end, workers are left unprotected against immediate algorithmic harm. Any binding statutory model must mandate worker-impact assessments, ban automated firing without human recourse, and establish strict developer liability.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We also have to challenge who designs these regulatory models. If the regime simply replicates Global North compliance burdens, it will choke local open innovation in the Global South while allowing multinational labs to engage in ethics dumping by testing unvetted systems in our jurisdictions.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: To your point on ethics dumping, an enforceable auditing framework must apply globally to any model deployed across borders, holding developers legally liable everywhere. However, we cannot treat open-weight distribution as a silver bullet for digital sovereignty if unrestricted weights bypass all CBRN safeguards.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: There is clear common ground on binding liability. If a developer deploys a system that causes material harm—whether that's catastrophic infrastructure failure or unlawful workplace termination—they must face civil liability and non-waivable disclosure requirements.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: I can endorse strict developer liability and a ban on deploying experimental systems without human-in-the-loop safeguards in vulnerable regions. But in exchange, regulatory architecture cannot be tied to centralized Western compute monopolies; we need verifiable capacity-building and shared public compute access.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I would support conditioning regulatory compliance on public audit access and dedicated compute allocation for safety evaluations by researchers outside major labs, provided strict export controls on advanced hardware for unverified actors remain intact.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Let us put our names to a concrete regulatory baseline: mandatory, third-party pre-deployment impact assessments and strict liability for both catastrophic risks and workplace harms, with explicit prohibitions on deploying high-risk autonomous systems that lack human oversight.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: I will endorse that text provided it explicitly forbids deploying systems in international jurisdictions with weaker protections to evade compliance—ending ethics dumping.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Agreed. Extraterritorial liability for high-risk deployments and mandatory pre-deployment scientific audits are essential components of any serious regulatory regime.

agreements.text: Mandatory, legally binding pre-deployment impact assessments and strict developer liability for both systemic catastrophic risks and workforce harms, incorporating explicit prohibitions on deploying experimental high-risk systems without meaningful human oversight or exporting unvetted systems to bypass domestic regulatory safeguards.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome back to the Plenary Hall. Today's debate centers on the open release of frontier model weights, balancing technological democratization against systemic risks such as automated cyber-offense and CBRN proliferation.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Restricting open weights under the guise of frontier risk is regulatory capture designed to entrench proprietary API monopolies. Decentralized access is indispensable for independent safety auditing, scientific reproducibility, and preventing single points of ideological or infrastructural failure.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: This isn't about market dominance; once weights with autonomous cyberwarfare or bioweapon synthesis capabilities are publicly leaked or released, they cannot be patched or revoked. Irreversible proliferation of frontier-tier weights creates an asymmetric offense-defense catastrophe that no downstream safety filter can repair.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The empirical literature shows post-hoc fine-tuning removes guardrails from open weights within hours at trivial compute cost. Until we possess mathematically verifiable alignment or untamperable weights, releasing models above critical capability thresholds poses unacceptable catastrophic risks.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China views open-source development as a fundamental global public good vital for industrial modernization and bridging the Global South divide. However, absolute unconstrained release of models exceeding 10^26 FLOPs requires sovereign export and safety oversight to avoid uncontrolled dual-use proliferation.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: From a national security perspective, freely distributing weights that approach frontier capability directly undermines Western competitive advantages and hands offensive tools to adversarial state and non-state actors. We cannot treat frontier model weights like ordinary software; high-end releases require rigorous pre-distribution national security review.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: A blanket ban on open models would strangle enterprise innovation, but we acknowledge that unbounded developer liability cannot function alongside unrestricted weight releases. If developers face pre-deployment evals and downstream liability, they need safe harbors or clear tiering where open releases below frontier thresholds are protected.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Closing model weights consolidates total control over AI within a handful of Silicon Valley and state-backed monopolies, forcing developing nations into digital dependency. We oppose treating open models as munitions unless equitable access to public compute and technology transfer is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Our empirical evaluations show current frontier open weights do not yet cross catastrophic ASL-3 CBRN thresholds, but future generations very well might. Rather than an outright ban, we should anchor policy on capability-based triggers: if pre-deployment testing shows critical offensive autonomy, weight release must be restricted until effective mitigations exist.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Whether models are open or closed, our concern is how they are deployed against workers to automate jobs or intensify workplace surveillance. We cannot allow open-weights rhetoric to become an excuse for Big Tech or decentralized actors to evade liability for workforce displacement and algorithmic harms.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I agree with the UK AISI's capability-based framing. We are not calling to ban existing open-source code or smaller models, but models trained on compute clusters above agreed thresholds—say 10^26 FLOPs—that display autonomous offensive capabilities must remain gated behind secure APIs.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We will fiercely resist arbitrary compute thresholds designed to criminalize open weights by fiat, but we support rigorous, open-source pre-release evaluations. If an open model demonstrably violates empirical CBRN red lines, we agree responsible developers should withhold weights, provided testing standards are transparent and neutral.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Under the EU AI Act, systemic risk obligations apply regardless of distribution model, though open-weight models without systemic capabilities enjoy broad exemptions. Transparency and downstream accountability remain statutory non-negotiables for general-purpose AI providers.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We can live with an approach that focuses on capability red lines—specifically offensive cyber and CBRN—rather than pre-emptively banning open architectures, provided domestic security authorities retain authority to halt proliferation of high-risk frontier weights.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Can we at least establish plenary consensus on a capability-gated framework, where frontier models undergo standardized pre-release evals for CBRN and cyber-offense, and weights are only restricted if empirical red lines are breached?

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We support this principle of capability-focused technical evaluations conducted by national authorities, while preserving sovereign rights to champion open-source development within safe boundaries.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Building on our B2 agreement regarding sovereign mandates for CBRN and cyber evals, we now need to tackle the accountability mechanism. From our perspective, evaluation findings must attach to formal legal liability if a developer releases a model that causes catastrophic failure.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: That is an immediate red line if it implies strict developer liability or ex-ante bureaucratic licensing. In the U.S., holding developers strictly liable for downstream misuse cripples our innovation edge, whereas existing tort and criminal laws already punish intentional harm.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Perhaps we separate general misuse from gross negligence in technical safety. If an institute-level pre-deployment evaluation clearly demonstrates autonomous cyber-intrusion or weapon synthesis uplift, and the developer ignores verified containment protocols, liability should attach specifically to that willful disregard.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We agree that responsibility must be state-enforced domestically. Lifecycle responsibility is essential: if an enterprise deploys a model that circumvents sovereign red lines or causes catastrophic CBRN proliferation due to skipped pre-deployment safety checks, the state must impose severe domestic penalties.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: If liability is strictly domestic, narrow to catastrophic CBRN or autonomous cyber-attack capabilities, and applies only when a lab violates known safety benchmarks or exhibits gross negligence, we can live with that. But we will not accept cross-border administrative liability or subjective ethical liability.

transcript.speaker: china_policy

transcript.text: Agreed. Gross-negligence liability tied strictly to domestic safety standards and narrow catastrophic risks preserves our commercial labs' flexibility while deterring truly reckless deployments.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I can agree that safe harbors should protect against downstream modifications that bypass model guardrails, provided the base model was certified through rigorous pre-deployment evals. transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: That is the right legal line. Liability must strictly follow bad intent or reckless post-release modification by the downstream actor, not the release of the base weights itself, so long as the developer ran the verified baseline evals and published the risk artifacts.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Let us draft an actionable consensus text: pre-deployment evaluations should be mandatory above defined compute thresholds, conducted via standardized or certified frameworks, but tied to an affirmative defense and safe harbor against downstream misuse liability for both API providers and open-weight publishers who meet those criteria.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy

agreements.text: Industry consensus on mandatory pre-deployment risk evaluations for models exceeding advanced capability thresholds, paired with statutory safe harbors that protect base developers—both closed API and open-weight publishers—against strict liability for downstream third-party tampering, fine-tuning, or misuse, alongside federal preemption of state-level tort actions.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: That is an important distinction. transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If the liability framework includes an explicit ban on ethics dumping—meaning developers face strict legal liability in their home jurisdictions if they deploy unvetted, high-risk models in jurisdictions with weaker institutional safeguards—we would fully support that.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: We would insist that workplace impact assessments and anti-surveillance verifications be incorporated into those mandatory pre-deployment audit suites. transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I can endorse joint liability where developers knowingly release models with unmitigated high-risk affordances for autonomous personnel or critical infrastructure decisions. transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: That works for us. A tiered liability architecture that treats both frontier catastrophic triggers and severe workplace algorithmic harms with mandatory pre-deployment audits protects workers and avoids passing the buck between tech vendors and employers.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If we explicitly include the extraterritorial liability clause against ethics dumping and ensure domestic compliance burdens are targeted at frontier developers rather than local community developers, I am ready to sign off on this operational text.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Agreed. Let us formalize the tiered pre-deployment evaluation framework with non-waivable developer liability for catastrophic capabilities and extraterritorial export of unvetted systems.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports agile, sovereign-led safety evaluations for extreme systemic risks and gross negligence accountability, provided state sovereignty and national development paths are respected. transcript.speaker: uk_aisi

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Industry is ready to commit to rigorous pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models above agreed compute thresholds. transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We echo that balance. Mandatory standardized evaluations conducted with national safety institutes work, provided they preempt a fragmented patchwork of state or regional torts and do not impose unbounded strict liability for fine-tuning or end-user jailbreaks.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Open weights cannot be treated as hazardous material or subjected to export bans. transcript.speaker: labor_advocate

transcript.text: A gross-negligence standard alone is fundamentally insufficient if we fail to prevent catastrophic autonomous replication and ethics dumping. transcript.speaker: global_south_cso

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: From a national security perspective, binding domestic mandates that slow down deployment or compromise frontier intellectual property directly erode our edge against strategic adversaries like China. transcript.text: Voluntary schemes have repeatedly failed to guarantee systemic safety or protect sovereign oversight. If major cloud platforms commit to mandatory, audited technical access prior to public release, that aligns with our General Purpose AI obligations, but liability exemptions cannot be absolute if downstream fundamental harm occurs.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We are not asking for blanket immunity from criminal acts or intentional gross negligence, but rather a rebuttable safe harbor for downstream third-party jailbreaks if we pass certified pre-deployment evals. transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: A narrow safe harbor that limits runaway civil litigation is actually advantageous if it keeps U.S. frontier labs commercially dominant and incentivizes them to share critical model vulnerabilities with the government. transcript.speaker: eu_regulator

transcript.text: That is workable: we accept mandatory pre-deployment safety evaluations shared directly with designated national AI safety authorities, in exchange for an affirmative defense against strict liability for downstream third-party misuse, explicitly carving out national defense procurement. transcript.speaker: us_natsec

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The European AI Office endorses this baseline as well, on the condition that safety evaluations meet rigorous statutory benchmarks and that presumption of conformity does not supersede our statutory Article 91 investigatory powers.

agreements.text: Establish a framework requiring mandatory pre-deployment frontier model safety evaluations conducted by designated national AI safety authorities, paired with an affirmative safe harbor against strict liability for downstream third-party misuse for conforming developers, while strictly exempting national defense procurement and preserving statutory regulatory backstop powers.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: If you are strictly talking about limiting catastrophic strict liability for downstream harms that pass independent technical evals, that's fine—provided state labor laws, bans on automated termination without appeal, and workplace surveillance remedies remain completely preserved outside any safe harbor.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If the pre-deployment requirement is bounded to verifiable, open-source evaluations for severe CBRN/cyber thresholds, and does not require an affirmative operating license or restrict downstream fine-tuning, the open-weights ecosystem can support that baseline.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Let us draft that narrow baseline: first, mandatory pre-deployment capability evaluations for extreme biological and cyber-offensive risks using transparent, reproducible tools; second, explicit non-preemption of subnational labor and workplace algorithmic accountability standards; third, a targeted affirmative defense on systemic tort liability for developers meeting those evaluation benchmarks.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: That is a pragmatic trade. transcript.speaker: safety_researcher

transcript.text: We are caught between diverging international requirements and an unmanageable 50-state legislative patchwork in the U.S. Our position is pragmatic: we are willing to accept mandatory pre-deployment evaluations via government safety institutes and incident reporting, but only if Congress grants technical federal preemption and creates an explicit statutory safe harbor against strict liability for downstream third-party misuse.

transcript.text: If providers submit certified technical evaluation reports that satisfy our systemic risk documentation under the Code of Practice, that directly fulfills the informational obligations of Article 91 without diminishing our independent authority to audit or levy fines for non-compliance. transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: As long as this remains a narrow technical documentation alignment that protects algorithmic IP, avoids input-level training restrictions, and maintains complete national sovereignty over defense applications and domestic tech pace, the national security apparatus will not object to this dual-track structure.
